{"id": "0b06996e-ebf3-431c-a8a2-7a966f5404c4", "role": "assistant", "block_type": "tool_summary", "content": [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "tooluse_pFZKD6iEztlA0ebisiEFag", "status": "success", "content": [{"text": "{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"Create your guardrail\",\"context\":\"# Create your guardrail\\n\\nAmazon Bedrock Guardrails offers filters that you can configure to\\nhelp avoid undesirable and harmful content and remove or mask sensitive information for\\nprivacy protection.\\n\\nYou can configure the following filters with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails:\\n\\n* **Content filters** \u2014 This filter helps you detect and filter harmful\\n text or image content in input prompts or model responses (excluding reasoning content). Filtering is done based\\n on detection of certain predefined harmful content categories: Hate, Insults,\\n Sexual, Violence, Misconduct and Prompt Attack. You can configure the filter\\n strength for each of these categories based on your use cases. With Standard tier, detection of undesirable content is extended to protect against harmful content within code elements including\\n comments, variable and function names, and string literals.\\n* **Prompt attacks** \u2014 Offered as a category within content filters, this filter can help you detect and\\n filter prompt attacks including jailbreaks, prompt injections, and prompt leakages (Standard tier only). This capability helps you detect prompts that are intended\\n to bypass content moderation, override instructions, or generate harmful content.\\n* **Denied topics** \u2014 You can define a set of\\n topics to avoid within your generative AI application. For example, a banking\\n assistant application can be designed to help avoid topics related to illegal\\n investment advice. With Standard tier,\\n content filters extend to code domains.\\n* **Word filters** \u2014 You can define a set of\\n custom words or phrases (exact match) that you want to detect and block in the\\n interaction between your users and generative AI applications. For example, you can\\n detect and block profanity (using a ready-to-use option) as well as specific custom words such as competitor\\n names, or other offensive words.\\n* **Sensitive information filters** \u2014 Can help\\n you detect sensitive content such as Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in\\n standard formats or custom regex entities in user inputs and FM responses. This filter is a probabilistic maching learning (ML)\\n based solution that is context dependent. It detects sensitive information based on the context within input prompts or model responses. Based on\\n your use case, you can block or mask inputs and responses containing sensitive information. For example, you can redact users' personal information while\\n generating summaries from customer and agent conversation transcripts.\\n* **Contextual grounding checks** \u2014 Can\\n\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-components.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Options for handling harmful content detected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails\",\"context\":\"# Options for handling harmful content detected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails\\n\\nYou can configure what actions your Amazon Bedrock guardrail takes at runtime when it detects\\nharmful content in prompts (`inputAction`) and responses\\n(`outputAction`).\\n\\nGuardrails filtering policies support the following actions when harmful content is\\ndetected in model inputs and responses:\\n\\n* **Block** \u2013 Block the content and replace it with\\n blocked messaging.\\n* **Mask** \u2013 Anonymize the content and replace it with\\n identifier tags (such as `{NAME}` or `{EMAIL}`).\\n\\n This option is available only with sensitive information filters. For more\\n information, see Remove PII from conversations by using sensitive information filters.\\n* **Detect** \u2013 Take no action but return what the\\n guardrail detects in the trace response. Use this option, known as\\n *detect mode*, to help evaluate whether your guardrail is\\n working the way that you expect\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-harmful-content-handling-options.html\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Class: Aws::Bedrock::Types::GuardrailPiiEntityConfig\\n \\n \u2014 AWS SDK for Ruby V3\",\"context\":\"### #**input_action** \u21d2 String\\n\\nSpecifies the action to take when harmful content is detected in the\\ninput. {"id": "20c34660-56e1-488a-bcd4-0b860099049b", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "**Probably yes, but you can't conclude it from that entry alone.** Several other things decide whether it's true.

**What the entry tells you**
- `action: BLOCK` is the original, combined setting for a PII entity. The newer config adds `inputAction`, `outputAction`, `inputEnabled` and `outputEnabled`, which let you set input and output separately.
- This entry has none of those four fields. I believe the combined `action` then applies to both prompts and responses, but the docs I found don't say so explicitly. This is an inference.
- If the customer had set the newer fields, say `inputAction: NONE` or `inputEnabled: false`, SSNs in prompts would not be blocked. Your entry has no such override, so that isn't the case here.
- The docs confirm that a BLOCK action replaces the content with the guardrail's blocked message. When the input is what triggers it, the request shouldn't reach the model.

**What the entry can't tell you**
1. **Whether the guardrail is attached to their requests.** A guardrail has no effect unless the application passes it on each call. That means the guardrail identifier and version on `Converse` or `InvokeModel`, or calling `ApplyGuardrail`. Ask for a sample request or their code.
2. **Which version is in use.** `GetGuardrail` returns the DRAFT by default. If the app calls a numbered version, that version may have been created before the policy was added. Ask them to run `GetGuardrail` with the specific `guardrailVersion`.
3. **Streaming mode.** In asynchronous streaming mode, the guardrail checks the response while it streams, so don't rely on it to block output before it reaches the user. Ask whether they use streaming and which mode.
4. **Detection isn't guaranteed.** AWS describes the sensitive information filter as probabilistic and ML-based, and it depends on context. Common SSN formats will usually be caught. Unusual formats, such as digits split across text or written out in words, may not be. "Blocked before the model" is a reasonable expectation, not a guarantee.
5. **Other leaks.** The entry covers SSNs only. Other PII types or custom regex entities aren't covered unless they appear elsewhere in the policy. You said this is the only entry.

**Questions for the customer**
- Does the `GetGuardrail` output show the full entry exactly as you quoted it, with no `inputAction` or `inputEnabled` fields? Note that an API response can omit fields the console shows.
- Which `guardrailVersion` do their calls use?
- Can they send a trace or response from a test prompt containing a fake SSN? With the guardrail trace enabled, an input block shows up as `action: BLOCKED` under `inputAssessment`. The `stopReason` is `guardrail_intervened`.

That test is the most reliable way to settle it. If you can get one, I'm happy to help read the output.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
